title: State and props
intro: Props let a component receive data from its parent, while state lets a component remember data that can change over time. In this lesson, you will learn how useState, event handlers, immutable updates, and lifting state up work together to build interactive React components.
takeaways: Props come from a parent and should be treated as read-only, while state is owned and updated by a component.
useState gives a component a state value and a setter that causes React to render with the new value.
When the next state depends on the previous state, use the functional update form such as setCount(previous => previous + 1).
Never mutate arrays or objects stored in state; create new values with spread, map, filter, or similar operations.
Keep state minimal by lifting shared state to a common parent and calculating derived values instead of storing duplicate state.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between props and state?
options: Props are always numbers, while state is always strings
Props come from a parent and are read-only to the child, while state is owned and managed by a component
Props can change automatically, while state can never change
There is no meaningful difference between them
quiz.explanation: Props are values provided by a parent component. A child should treat them as read-only. State is managed by the component that owns it and can change over time.

quiz.question: Which is the correct way to pass an event handler to a button when you want it to run after a click?
quiz.explanation: Passing handleClick gives React the function to call when the click happens. Calling handleClick() during rendering would execute it immediately.

quiz.question: Why is this a useful state update for a counter?
quiz.explanation: The functional update receives the latest previous state and calculates the next value from it. This is the preferred pattern when the new state depends on the previous state.

quiz.question: What is the best approach when adding an item to an array stored in React state?
options: Call push directly on the existing state array
Create a new array, for example with the spread operator
Convert the array to a string first
quiz.explanation: React state should not be mutated directly. Creating a new array, such as [...previousItems, newItem], preserves the immutable update pattern.

quiz.question: A component has count state and needs to display whether count is even or odd. What is usually the best approach?
options: Create a second state variable for parity and update both manually
Pass parity through a completely separate component
quiz.explanation: Parity is a derived value because it can be calculated directly from count. Keeping it as separate state would duplicate information and create another value that could become inconsistent.

exercise.title: Build a stateful counter
exercise.task: Create an `App` component that renders a Counter interface with a count element using `data-testid="count"`, plus three buttons with the exact texts `+`, `−`, and `Reset`. The count must start at 0; clicking `+` increases it by 1, clicking `−` decreases it by 1 but must never take it below 0, and clicking `Reset` sets it back to 0. The `−` button must be disabled whenever the count is 0. Add a paragraph using `data-testid="parity"` that displays exactly `even` or `odd`, calculated directly from the count rather than stored as separate state. The tests will click the buttons with the course click helper, so make sure the buttons are real interactive React buttons.
exercise.hint: Keep only count in state and calculate parity from it. Use functional state updates for increment and decrement, and use the disabled prop on the minus button when count is zero.

tests.name: starts at zero and shows even
plus increments the count and updates parity
minus decrements the count
minus cannot take count below zero
reset returns the count to zero
minus becomes enabled after incrementing
